summaries.summary: Antonymy and synonymy are central lexical semantic relations whose distinction matters for Machine Translation and Textual Entailment but is challenging due to similar contexts.

Two predominant NLP approach families, co-occurrence models and pattern-based models, use distributional vector representations and DSMs to represent meaning vectors and determine semantic relatedness.
Co-occurrence models use weighted feature vectors or word embeddings from neural techniques or matrix factorization, addressing sparsity and achieving strong results in many NLP tasks.
Pattern-based models use lexico-syntactic surface patterns, with work by Justeson/Katz:91, Hearst:92, Lin2003, Roth2014, and Schwartz:15 distinguishing semantic relations.
The paper presents AntSynNET, hypothesizing that antonymous word pairs co-occur in lexico-syntactic patterns within sentences more often than synonymous pairs.
AntSynNET induces syntactic-path patterns between X and Y from a large-scale web corpus, adds a distance feature, encodes patterns with LSTM units, and improves over prior pattern-based methods.

The paper outlines sections on related work, AntSynNET, pattern induction, LSTM encoding, two classification models, baselines, dataset, experiments, results, feature effects, word embeddings, and conclusion.
This section describes AntSynNET, a pattern-based LSTM for distinguishing antonyms from synonyms, including pattern induction, LSTM encoding, and two classification approaches.
The method uses patterns as indicators of word pair co-occurrence, deriving lexico-syntactic tree patterns from simple paths between target lemmas in syntactic parse trees.
Path patterns represent each syntax-tree node with lemma, POS tag, dependency label, and distance label, where each parent-child step has distance 1 and ancestor nodes have distance 0.
Each node vector concatenates the four-feature vectors: lemma, POS, dependency, and distance embeddings.
The four vectors represent embeddings of lemma, POS tag, dependency label, and distance label, and the symbol denotes concatenation.
A pattern is a sequence of node vectors, and its pattern vector is encoded by applying a recurrent neural network.
An RNN models sequential data with state vectors, but long-term dependencies can cause gradient vanishing or exploding, so the methods use an LSTM network.
LSTM units use adaptive gating with an input gate, forget gate, output gate, and memory cell, formalized through equations for each time step.
W denotes a weight matrix, b denotes layer-specific bias terms, σ denotes the sigmoid function, and the LSTM output is computed from the output gate and memory cell.
The symbol denotes element-wise multiplication, and the methods use the last state h_k to represent the vector of a pattern.
Two models distinguish antonyms from synonyms: a pattern-based LSTM with logistic regression, and a combined model concatenating word and pattern vectors.
The pattern-based model induces patterns for a word pair from a corpus, feeds each pattern into an LSTM, and computes the word pair vector.
Eq. 12 computes the word pair vector as a frequency-weighted average of pattern vectors over the pattern set.
The word pair vector uses pattern frequencies, is fed into logistic regression, and predicts a positive antonymous pair if probability is larger than 0.5.
Inspired by Baroni:12 and Shwartz:16, the combined model uses both patterns and distribution of target pairs to create combined vector representations.
Eq. 14 defines the combined vector of a word pair as the concatenation of the two word vectors and the pattern vector.
The combined vector includes the vectors of word x, word y, and the pattern vector, and is fed into logistic regression to classify antonyms and synonyms.
Two pattern-based baseline methods, the distributional method and the distributed method, are introduced for comparison with AntSynNET.
The first baseline, R&SiW, applies Roth2014's vector space model combining standard lexico-syntactic patterns and discourse markers to represent word pairs.
Michael Roth computed R&SiW relation classification results for the test sets, with marker-based and pattern-based weights tuned on validation sets and other hyperparameters set as described.

The SP method by Schwartz:15 uses symmetric patterns of 3-5 tokens, filters them to 11 patterns, computes PPMI co-occurrence counts, applies smoothing, and uses two Lin2003 patterns for antonym representation.
Applying SP to the data uses pre-trained SP embeddings with 500 dimensions, cosine similarity of word pairs, and a Support Vector Machine with Radial Basis Function kernel.
Training uses existing large-scale antonym and synonym pairs from Nguyen:16, originally collected from WordNet BIBREF9 and Wordnik.

Patterns are extracted from corpus sentences, filtered below five occurrences, restricted to word pairs with at least five patterns, balanced at 1:1, and split into 70% train, 25% test, and 5% validation sets.

Experiments use the English Wikipedia dump from June 2016, spaCy, dLCE embeddings with 100 dimensions, 10-dimensional label embeddings, cross-entropy loss, Adadelta, Theano, dropout of 0.5, and 40 epochs.

Table 3 shows proposed models significantly outperform baselines for adjectives by > .06 F_1, improve nouns by .02 F_1 over R&SiW and .37 F_1 over SP, and have higher verb recall but not F_1 over R&SiW.

High recall supports the co-occurrence hypothesis, while sampled 5 pairs per population showed no true-prediction pattern overlap and false-prediction overlaps of 2, 2, and 4 patterns for noun, adjective, and verb classes.
The novel distance feature is integrated along the syntactic path to capture parent-child relationships at $distance = 1$ and ancestor-descendant relationships at $distance > 1$.
The distance feature is compared with the direction feature proposed by Shwartz:16, which represented dependency-label direction between two nodes in a path from X to Y.

Using the same dataset and patterns as Section "Overall Results" and replacing the distance feature by the direction feature, Table 4 shows the distance feature enhances performance more effectively across all word classes.
The models replace dLCE word embeddings with pre-trained GloVe word embeddings with 100 dimensions to compare their effects on the performance of the two proposed models.
Table 5 shows dLCE word embeddings outperform pre-trained GloVe word embeddings by around .01 $F_1$ for both AntSynNET models on adjective and verb pairs, and around .01 and .04 $F_1$ on noun pairs.

The paper presented AntSynNET, a novel pattern-based neural method to distinguish antonyms from synonyms, hypothesizing antonymous word pairs co-occur more often in lexico-syntactic patterns within a sentence.

Patterns derived from simple paths in a syntactic parse tree, a novel path distance feature, and two AntSynNET approaches using long short-term memory units or combined vector representations were fed into logistic regression for classification.

The proposed models significantly outperformed two baselines mainly in recall, the distance feature outperformed a direction feature, the embeddings outperformed state-of-the-art GloVe embeddings, and the models rely only on corpus data.
Michael Roth is thanked for helping compute the results of the R&SiW model on the dataset.
